doc.title: Quincy Jones — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Being at the birth of things: Soul Bossa Nova's piccolos and Jerome Richardson
summary: Baker asks whether so many firsts, like the piccolos and flute on Soul Bossa Nova, can be accidents. Jones says you have to be open to receive them, and talks about his brain operations.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Life philosophy: faith, karma and how to live

blocks.x: Because when I was looking back through and seeing, like two years before Roots came along, you were already talking about this, and how many of these other things? Like for instance, Soul Bossa Nova. Who in the hell else is going to put two piccolos over the top of a band? Or the thing you said that happened quite by accident, of a flute player coming in . . .
. . . on the top of that sound.
I can’t believe those things are purely accidental. I know it comes out in your life that way, but when you see them happening in this kind of repetitiveness, either – you’ve been touched.

It is, and that’s the thing you have to accept. It is, and you say, it’s not an accident, and that you just have to be open enough to receive the thing. It’s a mindset. The Nobel guys talk about the mechanism of the brain. I’ve had this sucker worked over. They probably took some of the cobwebs out where they went in there two times.
And both of those were low-percentages for recovery.
